title: Ash-Shams: the sun and her brightness
hookLine: eleven oaths by sun, moon, day, night, sky and earth (91:1–7)

cards: When did you last watch the sun actually go down? Not a glance through a windshield. The whole slow slide: the light going orange, then pink, the sky still glowing after the sun itself is gone.
Most people see about a hundred sunsets a year and look at maybe two. Ash-Shams, the surah before Al-Layl, won't let you skip it.
It opens with a string of oaths, one after another, and every one points at something you walk under every day and mostly ignore.

teach.h: SHAMS — THE SUN, AND DUHA, ITS LIGHT.
teach.b: Surah ninety-one begins, in Pickthall's translation: By the sun and his brightness. In Arabic the sun, shams, is grammatically feminine, which is why the title says her brightness; Pickthall's English says his.
The word for brightness, duha, you already know: it names the morning surah from a few days ago, the full light of mid-morning. Then the oaths keep coming. By the moon when it follows the sun.
By the day when it shows the sun's glory. By the night when it covers it. By the sky and the One who built it.
By the earth and the One who spread it out. By the soul and the One who shaped it.
Commentators count eleven things sworn by, more than in any other surah. Why swear at all?
In Arabic, an oath says: stop, look at this, what comes next matters. The things sworn by are witnesses. And look at the order.
It starts huge and far away, the sun, and moves steadily closer: moon, day and night, sky, earth, and last, the soul.

teach.h: FROM THE SUN DOWN TO THE SOUL.
teach.b: The whole universe, and then you, like a camera zooming from space down to a single face.
Where the zoom lands is tomorrow's lesson. Today is the zoom itself: the ordinary sky is worth an oath.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told a companion who was making the night prayer too long for the people behind him to recite shorter surahs, and a hadith in Muslim's collection names Ash-Shams among them.
Short enough for a tired crowd, big enough to hold the whole sky.

how: Ash-Shams is one of the short surahs often recited in the prayer, especially the evening and night prayers; many Muslims learn its run of oaths by heart as children.

o: the desert wind that blows before a storm
the full moon that marks the month's middle
the sun, and the surah that swears by it

games.q: what's inside the oaths — tap the pairs.

s: Ash-Shams contains more oaths than any other surah
commentators count eleven things sworn by in its opening verses.
an oath in the Qur'an is mainly a promise to do something
here it works like: stop, look at this. the things sworn by are witnesses to what comes next.
the oaths move from far away to close
sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth, and last of all the soul.

games.q: Ash-Shams swears by the sun, then by the moon. how does it describe the moon?
o: when it hides from the sun
games.why: the moon when it follows the sun (91:2). commentators say: rising after it, or shining with the light it borrows from it.

practice: Wherever you are, find the light: a window, a patch of sun on the floor, the glow of the sky. Look at it for a while, its color, where it falls, how it changes things.
If it's night, picture the last sunset you remember, as clearly as you can.

wordCard.voice: Ash-Shams. The sun, the name of Surah ninety-one, which opens with eleven oaths, from the sun down to the soul. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the sun, a feminine noun; the l of al- blends into the sh, so al-shams is said ash-shams.

carryVoice: Your line: by the sun. Eleven witnesses, and the first one is overhead every day. Tomorrow, where the zoom lands.
